---
title: "ML Models Exercise"
---

**Setup**
```{r}
#load libraries
library(here) #for directory handling
library(tidyverse) #for data handling
library(tidymodels) #for modeling
library(glmnet) #for modeling
library(ranger) #for modeling
library(corrplot) #for correlation

#load data
data <- readRDS(here("ml-models-exercise","module-10-data_clean.rds"))

#inspect variable types and check for any issues
glimpse(data)
summary(data)
```

**Preliminaries**
```{r}
#set a random seed for reproducibility
rngseed <- 1234
set.seed(rngseed)
```

**More processing**

```{r}
#check levels that exist within the variable RACE
unique(data$RACE)

#collapse 88 and 7 into a single category "3"
data <- data %>%
  mutate(RACE = as.character(RACE)) %>%   # temporarily convert to character
  mutate(RACE = ifelse(RACE %in% c("7", "88"), "3", RACE)) %>%  # recode
  mutate(RACE = factor(RACE))  # convert back to factor

#confirm RACE levels
unique(data$RACE)
```

**Pairwise correlations**

```{r}
#select continuous (numeric) variables
cont_data <- data %>%
  select(Y, DOSE, AGE, WT, HT)

#compute correlation matrix
cor_matrix <- cor(cont_data)

#view correlation matrix 
cor_matrix

#create correlation plot
pastel_cols <- colorRampPalette(c("#BFD7EA", "#FFFFFF", "#F7C6C7")) #set pastel colors
corrplot(cor_matrix,
         method = "color", #heatmap
         type = "upper", #shows only upper triangle
         col = pastel_cols(200),
         addCoef.col = "black", #adds correlation values on the plot
         tl.col = "black",
         tl.srt = 45)
```

**Feature engineering**

```{r}
#check HT and WT data
summary(data$WT) #probably in kg
summary(data$HT) #probably in m

#calculate BMI
data <- data %>%
  mutate(
    BMI = WT / (HT^2)
  )

#check BMI variable
summary(data$BMI)
```

**Model building**
**First fit**

```{r}
#define recipe: outcome is Y, predictors are all other variables
rec <- recipe(Y ~ ., data = data) %>%
  step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors()) #for handling non-numeric variables

##MODELING
#LINEAR MODEL
#define linear regression model
lm_mod <- linear_reg() %>%
  set_engine("lm")

#create workflow
lm_wf <- workflow() %>%
  add_model(lm_mod) %>%
  add_recipe(rec)

#fit model
lm_fit <- fit(lm_wf, data = data)

#LASSO MODEL
#define LASSO model with penalty = 0.1
lasso_mod <- linear_reg(penalty = 0.1, mixture = 1) %>%
  set_engine("glmnet")

#create workflow
lasso_wf <- workflow() %>%
  add_model(lasso_mod) %>%
  add_recipe(rec)

#fit model
lasso_fit <- fit(lasso_wf, data = data)

#RANDOM FOREST MODEL
#define random forest model (default settings)
rf_mod <- rand_forest(mode = "regression") %>%
  set_engine("ranger", seed = rngseed)

#create workflow
rf_wf <- workflow() %>%
  add_model(rf_mod) %>%
  add_recipe(rec)

#fit model
rf_fit <- fit(rf_wf, data = data)

##PREDICTIONS
#linear model predictions
lm_preds <- predict(lm_fit, new_data = data) %>%
  bind_cols(data %>% select(Y))

rmse(lm_preds, truth = Y, estimate = .pred)

#LASSO predictions
lasso_preds <- predict(lasso_fit, new_data = data) %>%
  bind_cols(data %>% select(Y))

rmse(lasso_preds, truth = Y, estimate = .pred)

#random forest predictions
rf_preds <- predict(rf_fit, new_data = data) %>%
  bind_cols(data %>% select(Y))

rmse(rf_preds, truth = Y, estimate = .pred)

#plot observed vs predicted; linear
ggplot(lm_preds, aes(x = Y, y = .pred)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(title = "Linear Model: Observed vs Predicted",
       x = "Observed Y",
       y = "Predicted Y")

#plot observed vs predicted; LASSO
ggplot(lasso_preds, aes(x = Y, y = .pred)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(title = "LASSO Model: Observed vs Predicted",
       x = "Observed Y",
       y = "Predicted Y")

#The linear model and LASSO produce very similar plots because the penalty applied in the LASSO model is relatively small (0.1). As a result, the coefficients are only slightly shrunk, and the model behaves very similarly to a standard linear regression. Since little regularization is occurring, both models generate nearly identical predictions and therefore similar observed vs predicted plots.

#plot observed vs predicted; random forest
ggplot(rf_preds, aes(x = Y, y = .pred)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(title = "Random Forest Model: Observed vs Predicted",
       x = "Observed Y",
       y = "Predicted Y")

#compute RMSE for each model
lm_rmse <- rmse(lm_preds, truth = Y, estimate = .pred)
lasso_rmse <- rmse(lasso_preds, truth = Y, estimate = .pred)
rf_rmse <- rmse(rf_preds, truth = Y, estimate = .pred)

#create summary table of RMSE values
rmse_table <- tibble(
  Model = c("Linear Model", "LASSO", "Random Forest"),
  RMSE = c(lm_rmse$.estimate,
           lasso_rmse$.estimate,
           rf_rmse$.estimate)
)

rmse_table
```

**Tuning the models**

```{r}
##LASSO
#create a recipe for the LASSO model
lasso_rec <- recipe(Y ~ ., data = data) %>%
  step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors()) %>%
  step_normalize(all_predictors())

#define the LASSO model
lasso_mod_tune <- linear_reg(
  penalty = tune(),
  mixture = 1
) %>%
  set_engine("glmnet")

#combine the recipe and model into a workflow
lasso_wf_tune <- workflow() %>%
  add_recipe(lasso_rec) %>%
  add_model(lasso_mod_tune)

#create a grid of 50 penalty values from 1e-5 to 1e2
lasso_grid <- tibble(
  penalty = 10^seq(-5, 2, length.out = 50)
)

#create an apparent resampling object
lasso_resamples <- apparent(data)

#tune the LASSO model across all penalty values in the grid
lasso_tune_res <- tune_grid(
  lasso_wf_tune,
  resamples = lasso_resamples,
  grid = lasso_grid,
  metrics = metric_set(rmse)
)

#collect the tuning results 
lasso_metrics <- collect_metrics(lasso_tune_res, summarize = FALSE)

lasso_metrics

#find the penalty value with the lowest RMSE
best_lasso <- lasso_metrics %>%
  arrange(.estimate) %>%
  slice(1)

best_lasso

#plot RMSE versus penalty (for the life of me could not figure how to get autoplot to work)
ggplot(lasso_metrics, aes(x = penalty, y = .estimate)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  scale_x_log10() +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(
    title = "LASSO Tuning Results",
    x = "Penalty",
    y = "RMSE"
  )

#I think the LASSO tuning results show that the model performs best when the penalty is very small because at that point it’s basically acting like a regular linear regression with almost no shrinkage. As the penalty increases, the model starts shrinking the coefficients more, which simplifies things but also removes useful information from the predictors. Because of that, the predictions get worse and the RMSE increases. I think the RMSE doesn’t go lower than the linear model because LASSO is still a linear method, so it can’t really do better than the ordinary least squares fit on the same data. Since we’re using apparent resampling and evaluating on the same data we trained on, the full linear model already gives the best possible fit, and adding any penalty just makes the model perform worse.

##RANDOM FOREST
#define random forest model
rf_mod_tune <- rand_forest(
  mtry = tune(),
  min_n = tune(),
  trees = 300,
  mode = "regression"
) %>%
  set_engine("ranger", seed = rngseed)

#create a recipe
rf_rec <- recipe(Y ~ ., data = data)

#create workflow
rf_wf_tune <- workflow() %>%
  add_recipe(rf_rec) %>%
  add_model(rf_mod_tune)

#create tuning grid
rf_grid <- grid_regular(
  mtry(range = c(1, 7)), #mtry from 1 to 7
  min_n(range = c(1, 21)), #min_n from 1 to 21
  levels = 7
)

#use apparent resampling 
rf_resamples <- apparent(data)

#run tuning
rf_tune_res <- tune_grid(
  rf_wf_tune,
  resamples = rf_resamples,
  grid = rf_grid,
  metrics = metric_set(rmse)
)

#collect unsummarized results 
rf_metrics <- collect_metrics(rf_tune_res, summarize = FALSE)

rf_metrics

#plot RMSE across the random forest tuning parameters
ggplot(rf_metrics, aes(x = mtry, y = .estimate, color = factor(min_n), group = min_n)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(
    title = "Random Forest Tuning Results",
    x = "mtry",
    y = "RMSE",
    color = "min_n"
  )
```

**Tuning with CV**
```{r}
##LASSO
#create 5-fold cross-validation repeated 5 times
folds <- vfold_cv(data, v = 5, repeats = 5)

#tune LASSO using cross-validation
lasso_tune_res_cv <- tune_grid(
  lasso_wf_tune,
  resamples = folds,   # <-- THIS is the only change
  grid = lasso_grid,
  metrics = metric_set(rmse)
)

#view summarized results
collect_metrics(lasso_tune_res_cv)

#plot tuning results (autoplot now works!)
autoplot(lasso_tune_res_cv)

##RANDOM FOREST
#tune random forest using cross-validation
rf_tune_res_cv <- tune_grid(
  rf_wf_tune,
  resamples = folds,   # <-- same change
  grid = rf_grid,
  metrics = metric_set(rmse)
)

#view summarized results
collect_metrics(rf_tune_res_cv)

#plot tuning results
autoplot(rf_tune_res_cv)

#I think the main reason the RMSE increased for both models when using cross-validation is because the models are now being evaluated on unseen data instead of the same data they were trained on. When we used apparent resampling before, the models were essentially being tested on the training data, so the performance looked much better than it actually was. With cross-validation, the models have to make predictions on new data, which gives a more realistic estimate of performance, so the RMSE increases. 
# 
# For the LASSO model, I still see that the best performance happens at very small penalty values. I think this is because when the penalty is close to zero, the LASSO behaves almost like a regular linear model and keeps most of the useful information from the predictors. As the penalty increases, the coefficients are shrunk more, which removes important information and leads to worse predictions.
# 
# For the random forest, I think it performed much better before because it is a very flexible model and was likely overfitting the training data. With cross-validation, that overfitting is penalized because the model is tested on unseen data, so its performance drops a lot. Compared to LASSO, the random forest now has a higher RMSE, which suggests it does not generalize as well in this case.
# 
# Overall, I think the LASSO model performs better because it has a lower RMSE under cross-validation, meaning it makes more accurate predictions on new data.
```
